lessons.title: Inside a clause

blocks.text: Find the verb first

Start with the finite verb: the word that carries tense and would change if the line moved into the past. In 'And every fair from fair sometime declines', that word is 'declines'. Then ask who or what declines; the answer, 'every fair', is the subject. Verse often delays its verb, and finding the verb first stops an inverted order from misleading you.
Objects and complements

A transitive verb passes its action to an object, a separate thing: rough winds shake 'the darling buds of May', and the head of that noun phrase is 'buds'. A linking verb such as 'be', 'seem' or 'become' takes a complement instead, which describes the subject itself. In 'Thou art more lovely and more temperate' the complement tells you what 'thou' is; nothing receives an action.
Clauses that cannot stand alone

A clause has its own subject and finite verb. An independent clause can stand as a sentence; a dependent clause opens with a subordinator such as 'when', 'if', 'because' or 'which' and leans on another clause. In Sonnet 130, 'If snow be white' is a condition waiting for its answer. Sonnet 29 stretches the same shape across eight lines: its 'When' clause holds the speaker's misery in suspense, and the main clause, 'Haply I think on thee', arrives only at line 10.

parts.text: in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes

blocks.text: Clauses inside clauses

Each finite verb anchors its own clause, so counting finite verbs is the quickest way to count clauses. 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds' holds three: the main clause 'Love is not love', the relative clause 'which alters', and the clause 'when it alteration finds', each with its own verb. Infinitives such as 'to serve' and participles such as 'despising' carry no tense and do not anchor a clause.

lessons.title: Joining two clauses

blocks.text: The comma splice

A comma marks a pause inside a sentence or sets off a dependent element; on its own it cannot hold two independent clauses. 'The vote was close, the motion failed' is a comma splice. Repair it with a full stop or a semicolon, or keep the comma and add a coordinating conjunction such as 'but' or 'so'. Douglass's 'You may rejoice, I must mourn' is a splice used on purpose: the abrupt join makes the two fates collide.
Semicolons and the missing verb

A semicolon joins independent clauses that the writer wants read as one movement of thought. It also keeps a series of clauses legible when each clause already contains a comma. Douglass states the verb once ('your celebration is a sham') and then leaves it out: 'your boasted liberty, an unholy license'. The comma marks where 'is' has been dropped, so the semicolons must do the heavier work of separating the clauses.
What a colon promises

A colon follows a complete clause and promises that what comes next will explain or specify it. 'The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes' keeps that promise. A colon between a verb and its object, as in 'The reasons were: cost and delay', breaks the rule, because 'The reasons were' is incomplete. Shakespeare ends line 2 of Sonnet 18 with a colon, and the lines that follow set out why summer falls short.
Name the relation

Coordinating conjunctions name the relation a comma leaves unstated: 'and' adds, 'but' and 'yet' contrast, 'so' gives a result, 'for' gives a reason. 'It was late, so we left' says why they left. A dash makes a sharper break than any of them. Lincoln's Bliss copy uses dashes to separate 'we can not dedicate' from 'we can not consecrate', forcing a pause before each stronger verb.

lessons.title: Actors and actions

blocks.text: Who did what

In the active voice the subject performs the action: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive makes the receiver the subject and builds the verb from 'be' plus a past participle; the actor, if it appears at all, moves into a 'by' phrase: 'The motion was rejected by the committee.' Seven words become five when the actor returns to the front, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.
The vanishing actor

The passive lets a writer delete the actor completely: 'Mistakes were made.' The sentence is grammatical and complete, and it assigns responsibility to nobody. That is honest when the actor is unknown or irrelevant, as in 'The temple was built in the second century'. It is evasive when the writer knows exactly who acted. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?
Verbs disguised as nouns

A nominalisation turns an action into a noun: 'decide' becomes 'a decision', 'review' becomes 'a review of'. The noun then needs a weak verb such as 'made' or 'conduct' to carry it, and the sentence gains words while losing force. Turning the noun back into a verb restores both: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' A good test for any draft is to make the main characters subjects and their actions verbs.
Cut what carries nothing

Dead words carry no meaning a reader would miss. 'Personal opinion' repeats itself; 'basically' and 'final' add nothing to 'true' and 'outcome'; 'In my opinion, it is true that' only announces a claim the sentence is about to make. Cut them and sixteen words become six. Count before and after: a revision that keeps the claim and loses words is an improvement you can measure.

lessons.title: Claim, grounds and warrant

blocks.text: Find the claim

Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, from The Uses of Argument (1958), starts with the claim: the conclusion the arguer wants accepted. Grounds are the facts offered in its support, here the cracked girders. The warrant is the general rule that licenses the step from those facts to that claim: damaged girders should not carry heavy loads. Everyday arguments usually state the claim and the grounds and leave the warrant for the reader to supply.

statements.text: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

blocks.text: The warrant does the work

Attacking a warrant is often stronger than attacking the grounds. Nobody disputes that the prints were on the knife; a defence lawyer asks whether prints show handling at the relevant time. When the warrant itself needs support, Toulmin calls that support backing: here, forensic research on how prints transfer and how long they last. Writing the warrant out shows you exactly what an argument assumes.

statements.text: The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
Forensic studies show that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact.

blocks.text: Qualifiers and rebuttals

A qualifier states how strongly the claim is made: 'probably', 'in most cases', 'almost certainly'. A rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would fail: 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home'. Both make an argument harder to knock down, because they concede in advance the exceptions an opponent would raise. A claim with no qualifier is asserted as certain, and a single counterexample sinks it.

statements.text: Harriet leads every poll by eight points.
Probably.
Harriet will win the election.
Unless rain keeps her supporters at home.
The air pressure is falling fast.
Very likely.
It will rain tomorrow.
Unless the front stalls over the coast.

blocks.text: Label a new argument

Labelling an argument means asking each statement what job it does. A particular observation is grounds. A general rule linking that observation to the conclusion is a warrant. The conclusion is the claim, and an 'unless' clause is a rebuttal. In the pricing argument the warrant is the general rule about prices, and the rebuttal allows that rising costs might justify the higher price even with fewer sales.

statements.text: Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.
Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
The price should return to its old level.
Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos

blocks.text: Where the speaker stands

Aristotle's Rhetoric names three proofs a speech can supply: ethos, the character of the speaker; pathos, the emotions of the audience; logos, the argument itself. Douglass speaks in 1852 as a man the holiday excludes, and the 'yours' and 'mine' of 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine' draw on that standing. Lincoln builds ethos differently, with 'we': the president speaks as one of the mourners, not above them.

spans.text: I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.
You may rejoice, I must mourn.
We have come to dedicate a portion of that field,
as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live.

blocks.text: Moving the audience

Pathos is persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses in its hearers. Douglass sets one sunlight against two outcomes. 'Stripes' are the marks of the whip, and placing them beside the audience's 'life and healing' makes the contrast physical. Lincoln's pathos is quieter: the dead gave 'the last full measure of devotion', and the living are asked to be worthy of it.

spans.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.
that from these honored dead we take increased devotion to that cause for which they gave
the last full measure of devotion

blocks.text: Arguing from a premise

Logos is the argument carried by the words themselves. Lincoln's opening dates the nation to 1776 and the Declaration of Independence rather than to the Constitution of 1787, and it names the founding premise: 'all men are created equal'. The war, he reasons, tests whether a nation built on that proposition 'can long endure'. The speech argues from premise to consequence before it consoles.

spans.text: Four score and seven years ago
our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and
dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
Now we are engaged in a great civil war,
testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.

blocks.text: The right moment

Kairos is the opportune moment: what makes an argument fit its occasion. Douglass, invited to speak at an Independence Day celebration in Rochester, turns the occasion into his subject: 'What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?' Lincoln speaks on the battlefield where the dead lie, four and a half months after the fighting, and 'We are met on a great battle-field of that war' uses the place itself as evidence.

spans.text: What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?
I answer, a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
We are met on a great battle-field of that war.

lessons.title: Figures of repetition and balance

blocks.text: Repeat the opening

Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses. The repetition sets up a frame, and attention moves to what changes inside it: best, worst, wisdom, foolishness. Dickens keeps the frame going for ten clauses before the sentence breaks into 'we had everything before us'. Douglass uses the same device with 'your', and each repetition points back at his audience.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

blocks.text: Set opposites side by side

Antithesis places opposed ideas in parallel grammatical form, so that the parallel sharpens the opposition. Lincoln contrasts 'we' with 'they' and 'say' with 'did' inside one frame ('what ___ ___ here'), so the speech enacts its own modesty: words matter less than deeds. Dickens's 'best' and 'worst' sit in the same slot of the same clause.

spans.text: The world will little note, nor long remember

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

blocks.text: Reverse the order

Chiasmus reverses the order of terms in its second half: man, slave / slave, man. When the same words return, as here, the stricter name is antimetabole. Douglass places the figure at the turning point of his Narrative, just before he fights back against Covey, so the grammar reverses as his life does. Draw lines between the matching words and they cross in an X, the Greek letter chi.
Three parallel members

A tricolon is a series of three parallel members. Lincoln's 'of the people, by the people, for the people' varies only the preposition, so each phrase adds a relation: government drawn from the people, run by them, serving them. His earlier sequence 'dedicate', 'consecrate', 'hallow' climbs from civic to sacred, a tricolon whose members grow in weight.

lessons.title: Metre and scansion

blocks.text: Count the syllables

Scansion starts with syllables. 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' has ten, and the beats fall on the even ones: I, -pare, to, sum-, day. An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one is an iamb, and five iambs make iambic pentameter, the line of English verse drama and of the sonnet. Metrical stress need not match speech: 'to' takes a beat here only because of where it stands.
Where the beats land

An iambic pentameter line has ten positions alternating weak and strong, so the strong positions are the even-numbered syllables. In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May' the beats land on 'winds', 'shake', 'dar-', 'buds' and 'May'. Spoken English rarely gives five equal stresses. 'Rough' is heavy too, and reading it with weight against the metre is part of the line's force.
A feminine ending

A line can carry an extra unstressed syllable after its last beat. 'That looks on tempests and is never shaken' ends 'NE-ver SHA-ken', and the final '-ken' trails off. This is a feminine ending. The line is still pentameter, because it keeps five beats; Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' has the same shape, and its unresolved last syllable suits an unresolved question.
Rising and falling feet

Reverse the iamb and you have a trochee, stressed then unstressed. The witches in Macbeth chant in trochaic tetrameter, four falling feet: DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Set that beside Dickinson's iambic 'And sings the tune without the words', also eight syllables and four beats. The count is the same, but one line falls and the other rises, and Shakespeare gives his supernatural speakers a metre unlike the iambic speech of his human characters.

lessons.title: Sound and image

blocks.text: Repeated consonants

Alliteration repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words, usually on stressed syllables. Shakespeare's 'sessions of sweet silent thought' has three, and their hiss is the sound of quiet. Keats opens 'To Autumn' with 'mists and mellow', two m sounds that slow the line. Alliteration belongs to sound, not spelling: 'cider' and 'sorrow' alliterate, 'cider' and 'cat' do not.
Repeated vowels

Assonance repeats a vowel sound in nearby stressed syllables, whatever the consonants around it. In 'Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness' the long vowel of 'bride' returns in 'qui-', binding the urn's two names together, while 'still' and 'unravish'd' keep the short i. Shakespeare's 'new wail my dear time's waste' sounds the vowel of 'wail' again in 'waste'.

model.source: Keats, 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', line 1

blocks.text: Like, or is

A simile compares openly, with 'like' or 'as': Burns's love is like a rose, and 'like' keeps the two apart. A metaphor identifies one thing with another: 'Juliet is the sun'. Romeo does not say she resembles the sun; he asserts it and then builds on the assertion, telling the 'fair sun' to 'kill the envious moon'. The metaphor makes a world in which its claim is true.

spans.text: But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?

blocks.text: Tenor and vehicle

I. A. Richards called the subject of a metaphor its tenor and the borrowed image its vehicle. Dickinson's tenor is hope, and her vehicle is a bird she leaves unnamed at first, letting 'feathers' and 'perches' imply it until 'the little bird' of the second stanza. Wordsworth keeps his comparison explicit: 'I wandered lonely as a Cloud'. Naming tenor and vehicle lets you say exactly what a figure carries across.

lessons.title: The sonnet and its turn

blocks.text: Three quatrains and a couplet

Shakespeare's sonnets have fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three quatrains and a closing couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. Each quatrain brings two new rhymes, so the poem moves through seven rhyme sounds and ends on a pair. In Sonnet 18 the quatrains test the comparison with summer, and the couplet answers it: 'So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.'

lines.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
When I consider how my light is spent,
E’re half my days, in this dark world and wide,
And that one Talent which is death to hide,
Lodg’d with me useless, though my Soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, least he returning chide,
Doth God exact day-labour, light deny’d,
I fondly ask; But patience to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, God doth not need
Either man’s work or his own gifts, who best
Bear his milde yoak, they serve him best, his State
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and waite.

blocks.text: Octave and sestet

The Italian or Petrarchan sonnet divides into an octave of eight lines rhyming ABBAABBA and a sestet of six, often CDECDE. Two rhyme sounds carry the whole octave. That demands four rhymes on each sound, which Italian supplies easily and English does not. Milton's 'When I consider how my light is spent' keeps the pattern: spent, wide, hide, bent, present, chide, deny'd, prevent.

I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,

I grant I never saw a goddess go;

And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,

blocks.text: The volta

The volta is the turn: the point where a sonnet changes direction, from problem to answer or from complaint to consolation. In the Petrarchan sonnet it usually falls where the octave gives way to the sestet. Sonnet 29 turns at that point too: eight lines of envy and self-pity, then 'Yet in these thoughts', and the speaker's state rises 'like to the lark at break of day arising'.

lines.text: When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes
I all alone beweep my outcast state,

And look upon myself, and curse my fate,
Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
Featur’d like him, like him with friends possess’d,
Desiring this man’s art, and that man’s scope,
With what I most enjoy contented least;
Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising,
Haply I think on thee, and then my state,
Like to the lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;
For thy sweet love remember’d such wealth brings
That then I scorn to change my state with kings.

Shakespeare often delays the turn to the couplet. Sonnet 130 refuses every flattering comparison for three quatrains and turns only with 'And yet by heaven', claiming that his love is as rare as any woman 'belied with false compare'. Milton turns early, in the middle of line 8: 'But patience to prevent / That murmur, soon replies'. Where the turn falls decides how much of the poem argues and how much answers.

lessons.title: Who sees and who speaks

blocks.text: First person and third

Grammatical person tells you where the narrator stands. A first-person narrator is a character who says 'I', as Poe's does: 'why will you say that I am mad?' A third-person narrator stands outside the story and calls the characters 'he' and 'she'. Emma opens in the third person, and the word 'seemed' already hints that this narrator knows more than Emma does.

spans.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence;
True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

blocks.text: A narrator who knows more

An omniscient narrator can generalise beyond any one mind. Pride and Prejudice opens with a 'truth universally acknowledged' and reveals in the next paragraph whose truth it is: the 'surrounding families', who regard a rich newcomer as 'the rightful property' of their daughters. The narrator borrows the neighbourhood's voice in order to expose it, and the wanting runs the other way from what the sentence claims.

spans.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged,
that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as
of some one or other of their daughters.

blocks.text: Free indirect discourse

Free indirect discourse renders a character's thought in the narrator's grammar, third person and past tense, while keeping the character's idiom and feeling. 'It was a wretched business indeed!' is Emma's exclamation, not the narrator's verdict: 'indeed' and the exclamation mark are hers. Austen moves in and out of Emma's mind without signalling the shift, so readers share her mistakes before they recognise them as mistakes.

spans.text: The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
It was a wretched business indeed!
“If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
How she could have been so deceived!

blocks.text: Sorting the three modes

Two questions sort the modes: who is speaking, and whose words are these? Quotation marks and 'I' mark direct speech. Actions reported from outside, such as 'the maid sent away', are narration. A third-person sentence that carries the character's own exclamation, question or idiom, such as 'How she could have been so deceived!', is free indirect discourse.

spans.text: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
(2) The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
(3) How she could have been so deceived!
Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!
She looked back as well as she could;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish first- from third-person narration and hear an omniscient narrator's irony. Recognise free indirect discourse in Austen.

lessons.title: Irony and unreliable narrators

blocks.text: Saying the opposite

Verbal irony says one thing and means another, and the audience must be able to hear the gap. Antony calls Brutus 'an honourable man' four times in these lines, each time after evidence that Caesar was not ambitious: the captives' ransoms, the refused crown. By the last repetition the word has turned against Brutus, and the crowd has done the turning.

spans.text: So are they all, all honourable men,
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, and so his charge that Caesar was ambitious must be true.
model.known: Brutus helped kill Caesar, and each repetition invites the crowd to doubt the word.

blocks.text: The audience knows

Dramatic irony depends on unequal knowledge. Romeo marvels that death 'hath had no power yet upon thy beauty', and the audience knows why: Juliet is not dead. Every line he speaks means more to us than to him. Duncan's praise of Macbeth's home, 'This castle hath a pleasant seat', works the same way, spoken by a king the audience knows will be murdered inside it.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: Death that hath suck’d the honey of thy breath, / Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty.
model.said: Juliet is dead, and her beauty is death's strange mercy.
model.known: Juliet has taken the Friar's sleeping potion and is about to wake.

model.speaker: Duncan
model.line: This castle hath a pleasant seat.
model.said: The castle is a welcoming place to rest.
model.known: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth have resolved to murder Duncan there that night.

blocks.text: When events turn

Situational irony lies in events: an outcome reverses the intention or expectation that produced it. Romeo steps in to make peace and so gives Tybalt his opening, and his reply to the dying Mercutio, 'I thought all for the best', names the gap between purpose and result. Situational irony needs no speaker and no hidden knowledge, only an outcome that turns against its cause.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: I thought all for the best.
model.said: Stepping between the fighters will stop the duel.
model.known: Tybalt's thrust under Romeo's arm kills Mercutio: the peace-making makes the death possible.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And sure he is an honourable man.
model.known: Antony means the opposite, and the crowd hears it.

blocks.text: A narrator to distrust

An unreliable narrator gives an account the reader learns to doubt, often from evidence inside the telling. Poe's narrator protests his calm in sentences broken by dashes and repetition, and he offers his acute hearing ('I heard many things in hell') as proof of sanity. The reader reads past him and assembles a second story from what he lets slip. Wayne Booth named the type in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961).

spans.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am;
but why will you say that I am mad?
I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell.
Object there was none. Passion there was none.

lessons.orientation: Tell verbal, dramatic and situational irony apart, and read past a narrator whose account gives itself away.

lessons.title: Structure: arcs and turning scenes

blocks.text: Freytag's pyramid

Gustav Freytag's Die Technik des Dramas (1863) divides a five-act play into five parts: introduction, rise, climax, return or fall, catastrophe. In Romeo and Juliet he traces the rise through four stages (the masked ball, the garden, the wedding, Tybalt's death) and sets the climax in Act 3, from Juliet's 'Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds' to Romeo's farewell. Everything after that descends towards the tomb.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

blocks.text: Exposition and the first impulse

The opening part, which English critics usually call the exposition, sets out the world before the action starts. For Freytag that means an Italian city where swords are worn and quarrels flare; the heads of the two houses; a prince who keeps the peace with difficulty. It ends at what he calls the exciting moment, the impulse that starts the action: Romeo and his friends deciding to go to the Capulet feast.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

blocks.text: Scenes that turn

A play turns scene by scene as well as act by act. Give each scene a value for the protagonists, hope or loss, at its start and its end. A scene that changes the value turns; one that does not builds or confirms. On this reading of Romeo and Juliet the turns cluster after the wedding: Tybalt's death, the parting, the potion, the false news in Mantua. The tomb opens in loss and stays there.
Find the climax

Freytag's pyramid gives a quick test for any plot: find the highest point, where the protagonist's fortunes stop rising and start to fall. In this heist the alarm is the climax; the chase and the split are falling action, and the last scene works as the catastrophe or resolution. Comedies use the same shape with the ending reversed, rising again to a marriage or a reunion.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lessons.orientation: Map a play onto Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes that turn a value from hope to loss or back.

questions.prompt: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 says 'And every fair from fair sometime declines.' Which single word is the finite verb?
hints: Put the line into the past tense. Which word changes form?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Declines' is the finite verb: it carries tense and would become 'declined' in the past. Its subject is 'every fair'.

questions.prompt: In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May', the object is a noun phrase. What is its head noun, the one word the rest of the phrase describes?
hints: Strip away the describing words. Which noun is left as the thing being shaken?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object is 'the darling buds of May'; its head noun is 'buds'. 'Darling' and 'of May' modify it.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 has 'If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.' Which word makes the first clause dependent?
hints: Which word turns a statement into a condition?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'If' subordinates 'snow be white', so that clause cannot stand alone; 'her breasts are dun' can.

questions.prompt: How many finite verbs are in 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds'?
hints: A finite verb carries tense: test each word by putting the lines into the past.
Check the main clause, then the clause opened by 'which', then the clause opened by 'when'.
List one verb from each clause and count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'is', 'alters' and 'finds'. Each anchors a clause.

questions.prompt: Douglass, 1852: 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' How many independent clauses does this sentence hold?
hints: Find each subject and finite verb pair.
Ask whether each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.
Neither clause opens with a subordinator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'You may rejoice' and 'I must mourn'. Each could stand alone, and the comma between them is a deliberate splice.

questions.prompt: In Lincoln's 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here', what is the grammatical function of 'what we say here'?
hints: Ask: the world will little note what? The answer names the object.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'What we say here' is a noun clause that receives the action of 'note' and 'remember', so it is their object. The subject is 'the world'.

questions.prompt: 'The vote was close, the motion failed.' Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone. What do editors call this construction?
hints: The name pairs the mark with a word from rope-work and film editing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma splice: in edited prose a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which verb is understood but not repeated in the second and third clauses?
hints: Read the first clause, then lend its verb to the second.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Is': each later clause means 'your boasted liberty is an unholy license'. The comma marks where the verb was left out.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
hints: Test the words before each colon: could they stand as a sentence?

acceptedIdeas: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A colon needs a complete clause before it, and what follows should explain or specify. Only the first sentence meets both conditions.

choices.label: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
The motion: failed by two votes.
The reasons were: cost and delay.

questions.prompt: Repair 'It was late, we left' by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction that states cause and result. Which conjunction do you add?
hints: The second clause is the result of the first. Which short word introduces a result?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'So': 'It was late, so we left.' 'And' would join the clauses without naming the cause.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' Keeping the comma, which coordinating conjunction would make this standard edited prose while keeping the contrast?
hints: Choose the conjunction that sets one clause against the other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'But' or 'yet': 'You may rejoice, but I must mourn.' Both name the contrast; 'and' would flatten it.

questions.prompt: How many independent clauses are in 'The hall was full; the speaker was late: his train had stopped outside the city.'?
hints: Find each subject with its finite verb.
Check whether any clause opens with a subordinator such as 'because' or 'when'.
Each mark here separates complete clauses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'The hall was full', 'the speaker was late' and 'his train had stopped outside the city'. The colon introduces the reason for the lateness.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'The motion was rejected by the committee' in the active voice. How many words does the active sentence have?
hints: Make the actor, the committee, the subject.
Use the past-tense verb without 'was', and drop 'by'.
Count every word, including both articles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive took seven.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'Mistakes were made by the finance office' in the active voice. What becomes the subject?
hints: Find the 'by' phrase: whoever sits inside it performed the action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The finance office made mistakes.' The actor, hidden in the 'by' phrase, moves into the subject position.

questions.prompt: Unbury the verbs in 'The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy': 'made a decision' becomes 'decided' and 'conduct a review of' becomes 'review'. How many words does the revision save?
hints: Count the words in the original sentence.
Write out the revision and count it.
Subtract the revised count from the original count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve words become seven: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' Five are saved.

questions.prompt: Cut the empty frame 'In my opinion, it is true that' and the redundant words 'personal', 'basically' and 'final' from 'In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.' How many words remain?
hints: Count the original sentence first.
Count the frame words and the redundant words you are removing.
Subtract, then check by reading what is left aloud.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sixteen words lose ten: 'The outcome depends on the weather.' Six remain.

questions.prompt: 'The budget was approved by the council in March.' How many words does the active version save?
hints: Put the council in the subject position.
Write the active sentence and count it.
Subtract the active count from the passive count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine words become seven: 'The council approved the budget in March.' Two are saved.

questions.prompt: 'An investigation of the causes was carried out by the board.' Which verb is buried inside the noun 'investigation'?
hints: Remove the noun ending '-ation' and rebuild the verb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Investigate': 'The board investigated the causes' turns the noun back into a verb and the board into the subject.

questions.prompt: Three statements: 'Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.' 'The bridge should close to lorries.' 'A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.' Which is the claim?
hints: Ask which statement the others are reasons for.

acceptedIdeas: The bridge should close to lorries.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The bridge should close to lorries' is the conclusion the other two statements are offered to support.

choices.label: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.

questions.prompt: Grounds: 'The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.' Claim: 'The defendant handled the knife.' What is Toulmin's name for the unstated rule 'Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it'?
hints: The element authorises the step from evidence to conclusion; the same word names a document that authorises a search.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant: the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

questions.prompt: In 'Harriet will probably win, unless rain keeps her supporters at home', which single word is the qualifier?
hints: Find the word that measures how confident the claim is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Probably' limits the force of the claim; 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home' is the rebuttal, the condition under which it fails.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise. (2) Customers buy less of a product when its price rises. (3) The price should return to its old level. (4) Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen. Give the number of the statement that is the warrant.
hints: Find the claim first: the statement the others support.
Find the observed fact; that is the grounds.
The warrant is a general rule rather than a particular fact.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure (grounds, statement 1) to the pricing claim (statement 3). Statement 4 is the rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) The museum should open late every Thursday. (2) Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late. (3) A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost. (4) The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last. Give the number of the statement that supplies the grounds.
hints: Find the statement the others support.
Grounds are particular observed facts, not general rules.
The last statement limits the argument rather than supporting it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 supplies the grounds: an observed fact. Statement 1 is the claim, 3 the warrant and 4 a rebuttal.

questions.prompt: A writer supports the warrant 'Damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads' by citing the national bridge inspection code. In Toulmin's model, what is that support called?
hints: The support is aimed at the rule, not at the conclusion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Backing: support for the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

questions.prompt: Douglass tells his Rochester audience, 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.' His right to say it rests on his own life as a man who had escaped slavery. Which of Aristotle's appeals works through the speaker's character and standing?
hints: The Greek word is the root of 'ethics'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: the persuasive force of the speaker's character and credibility.

questions.prompt: 'The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.' The image of 'stripes and death' is aimed chiefly at the audience's feelings. Which appeal is this?
hints: The Greek root also gives English 'sympathy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: the appeal to the audience's emotions, here pity and shame.

questions.prompt: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863. 'Four score and seven years ago' points back to which year?
hints: A score is twenty.
Four score and seven is four twenties plus seven.
Subtract that number of years from the year of the speech.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.prompt: Douglass delivered his attack on slavery at a celebration of American independence, the day after the Fourth of July. Which Greek term names a speaker's use of the right moment and occasion?
hints: It is the term often added to Aristotle's three appeals, and it means the opportune moment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kairos: the timeliness of a speech, the fit between argument and occasion.

questions.prompt: Lincoln says the war is 'testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.' He reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake. Which appeal is this chiefly?
hints: Look for the appeal named after the Greek for 'word' or 'reason'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos: an appeal through reasoning from premise to consequence.

questions.prompt: A charity letter opens: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years, I have seen what a missed vaccination can do.' Which appeal does the opening clause make first?
hints: Look at what the opening clause tells you about the writer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years' establishes the writer's experience and credibility before anything else.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.' How many times does 'it was' open a clause in this extract?
hints: Split the extract at each comma.
Mark the first two words of each clause.
Count the clauses that open the same way.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora; in the full sentence Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses.

questions.prompt: Lincoln sets 'what we say here' against 'what they did here' in matching grammatical form. Name the figure that balances opposed ideas in parallel structure.
hints: The Greek name means 'setting against'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Antithesis: contrasting ideas placed in parallel form, here saying against doing and 'we' against 'they'.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.' The terms return in reverse order, A B B A. Name the figure.
hints: The name comes from the Greek letter chi, shaped like an X.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

questions.prompt: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.' Name the figure made of three parallel members.
hints: The Greek prefix for three is joined to the word for a clause or limb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which figure does the repeated opening 'your' create?
hints: Repetition at the start of successive clauses has a name from the Greek for 'carrying back'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair.' Which figure is this?
hints: Look at the order of the two repeated words in each half.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus: fair, foul / foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'
hints: Say the line slowly and tap once for each vowel sound.
'Compare' and 'summer's' have two syllables each.
Every other word has one syllable; add them up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: shall / I / com / pare / thee / to / a / sum / mer's / day.

questions.prompt: In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables. Counting from the first syllable, on which syllable does the third beat fall?
hints: List the syllable positions that carry beats.
The first beat falls on the second syllable.
Each further beat comes two syllables later.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'That looks on tempests and is never shaken'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Tempests', 'never' and 'shaken' have two syllables each.
Notice what follows the last beat on 'sha-'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eleven. '-ken' is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat on 'sha-': a feminine ending.

questions.prompt: The witches chant 'Double, double, toil and trouble': DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Each foot falls from stressed to unstressed. Name this foot.
hints: Its Greek name means 'running'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Dickinson's 'That perches in the soul'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Perches' has two syllables.
Count the remaining one-syllable words and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: that / per / ches / in / the / soul. Three iambs make iambic trimeter.

questions.prompt: A line has four iambic feet, as in 'And sings the tune without the words'. Name its metre: iambic what?
hints: The Greek prefix for four comes before '-meter'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Iambic tetrameter: four iambs, eight syllables.

questions.prompt: In 'When to the sessions of sweet silent thought', how many words begin with the s sound?
hints: Read the line aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore s sounds in the middle or at the end of words.
Check the nouns and adjectives one by one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'sessions', 'sweet' and 'silent'. The hushed s sounds suit a line about silent thought.

questions.prompt: In Keats's 'Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness', how many words contain the long vowel heard in 'bride'?
hints: Listen to vowel sounds rather than letters: 'still' has a short vowel.
Say 'quietness' slowly: qui-et-ness.
Count every word whose vowel matches the one in the model word, including that word itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'bride' and 'quietness' (qui-). 'Still' and 'unravish'd' have the short vowel of 'sit'.

questions.prompt: Burns: 'O my Luve's like a red, red rose.' The comparison is made with 'like'. Name the figure.
hints: The figure announces itself as a comparison; its name shares a root with 'similar'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.prompt: In Dickinson's 'Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul', hope is pictured as a creature. Which creature is implied?
hints: It has feathers and perches, and in the next lines it sings.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bird: the feathers, the perching and later the singing belong to it, and the second stanza names 'the little bird'.

questions.prompt: Wordsworth: 'I wandered lonely as a Cloud.' Name the figure.
hints: Look for the word that announces a comparison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: 'as' makes the comparison between the speaker and the cloud explicit.

questions.prompt: Romeo: 'It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!' Which statement is accurate?
hints: Is there a 'like' or an 'as'?

acceptedIdeas: It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A metaphor: Romeo identifies Juliet with the sun rather than comparing her with 'like' or 'as'.

choices.label: It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun
It is a simile, because two things are compared
It is alliteration on the s sound

questions.prompt: A Shakespearean sonnet rhymes ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. How many different rhyme sounds does that scheme use?
hints: Each letter stands for one rhyme sound.
List the letters without repeats.
Count the distinct letters from A onward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven, A to G: three quatrains bring two new rhymes each, and the couplet adds one.

questions.prompt: Milton's sonnet on his blindness opens with an octave rhyming ABBAABBA. How many rhyme sounds does the octave use?
hints: Each letter is one rhyme sound.
Ignore repeats of a letter.
Count the distinct letters in the octave's scheme.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: A (spent, bent, present, prevent) and B (wide, hide, chide, deny'd).

questions.prompt: At which line does Sonnet 29 turn from despair to consolation?
hints: Find the first word that changes the direction of the argument.
Look at the opening of the third quatrain.
Count the lines down to that word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 9: 'Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising'. 'Yet' turns the poem after two quatrains of complaint.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 spends its quatrains mocking conventional comparisons. At which line does it turn?
hints: Find the words that reverse the poem's direction.
Look where the closing couplet begins.
Count the lines in the three quatrains, then add one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 13: 'And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare'. The couplet carries the turn.

questions.prompt: Milton turns inside line 8: 'I fondly ask; But patience to prevent / That murmur, soon replies'. Which personified quality answers the speaker?
hints: Read the words after 'But' in line 8.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Patience: it interrupts the complaint and answers it in the sestet, ending 'They also serve who only stand and waite.'

questions.prompt: How do a Shakespearean sonnet's final two lines usually work?
hints: The scheme ends with a repeated letter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rhyming couplet, GG, often carrying the turn or the answer to the quatrains.

questions.prompt: Austen opens Emma: 'Emma Woodhouse … seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.' In which grammatical person is this narration?
hints: Does the narrator say 'I', or describe Emma from outside?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third person: the narrator names Emma and refers to her as 'she', standing outside the story.

questions.prompt: Whose view does 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife' express?
hints: No character has yet appeared when the sentence is spoken.

acceptedIdeas: The narrator, voicing a neighbourhood's assumption with irony
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The narrator states the assumption as if it were universal; the next paragraph shows it belongs to families with daughters to marry.

choices.label: The narrator, voicing a neighbourhood's assumption with irony
Mr Bennet, speaking to his wife
Elizabeth Bennet, in her private thoughts

questions.prompt: After Mr Elton's proposal Austen writes: 'Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!' The second sentence is Emma's own exclamation, in the third person and past tense, with no 'she thought' and no quotation marks. What is this technique called?
hints: Compare it with 'She thought that it was a wretched business'. Which part has been dropped, and what does that make the reported thought?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse, also called free indirect style or speech: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice.

questions.prompt: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.” (2) … Emma sat down to think and be miserable. (3) How she could have been so deceived! Give the number of the sentence that is free indirect discourse.
hints: Direct speech sits inside quotation marks.
Plain narration reports actions from outside.
Look for a character's exclamation in the third person.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sentence 3: Emma's exclamation in the third person and past tense, with no reporting verb. Sentence 1 is direct speech; sentence 2 is narration.

questions.prompt: Turn the direct thought 'I have been a fool' into free indirect discourse about Emma. Which pronoun replaces 'I'?
hints: Free indirect discourse uses the narrator's grammatical person, not the character's.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'She had been a fool!' The person shifts to the third and the tense moves back, but the exclamation stays Emma's.

questions.prompt: Which feature most reliably marks free indirect discourse?
hints: Think about what is missing compared with 'she thought that'.

acceptedIdeas: A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse keeps the narrator's person and tense but drops the reporting verb, so the character's idiom enters the narration directly.

choices.label: A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb
Quotation marks around a character's words
A first-person narrator addressing the reader

questions.prompt: In the eight lines shown from Antony's funeral speech, how many times is Brutus called 'an honourable man'?
hints: Look for the exact phrase with the singular 'man'.
'All honourable men' refers to the conspirators as a group; leave it out.
Count each line that applies the phrase to Brutus, including the one that calls him 'he'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so the praise turns into accusation: verbal irony.

questions.prompt: Romeo, in the tomb, believes Juliet is dead; the audience knows she has taken a sleeping potion and will wake. What kind of irony arises when the audience knows what a character does not?
hints: It is named after the form in which it is most at home: plays.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience's knowledge exceeds the character's, so his words carry a meaning he cannot hear.

questions.prompt: Romeo steps between Mercutio and Tybalt to stop the fight, and Tybalt's thrust under his arm kills Mercutio. The intervention causes the death it was meant to prevent. Which kind of irony is this?
hints: The irony lies in how events turn out, not in what anyone says or knows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Situational irony: the outcome reverses the intention that produced it.

questions.prompt: Poe's narrator insists he is sane while describing a murder in frantic, broken sentences. What term describes a narrator whose account readers have reason to distrust?
hints: It is the opposite of a narrator whose word you can trust.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An unreliable narrator: the telling itself, with its dashes and protests, gives evidence against what it claims.

questions.prompt: Austen's narrator calls it 'a truth universally acknowledged' that a rich single man 'must be in want of a wife'; the novel shows it is the families who want the man. Which kind of irony does the sentence use: dramatic, situational or verbal?
hints: The irony lives in the wording of a statement.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the statement says one thing and means its reverse.

questions.prompt: In a play, the audience has watched a character poison the wine. The host then raises a glass and toasts his guest's long life. Which kind of irony is at work?
hints: Ask who knows about the poison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience knows about the poison and the host does not, so his toast means something he cannot hear.

questions.prompt: Romeo and Juliet has five acts. In which act does Freytag place its climax, the high point after which the action turns against the lovers?
hints: Freytag's pyramid puts the climax in the middle of a five-act play.
Find the act in which Romeo kills Tybalt and the lovers part.
Count the acts up to that point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Act 3. Freytag treats Tybalt's death as the end of the rise and the scene group from 'Gallop apace' to Romeo's farewell as the climax.

questions.prompt: Name the part of Freytag's pyramid that introduces the place, the time and the people before the conflict begins.
hints: It comes first and explains the situation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The exposition, Freytag's 'Einleitung' or introduction.

questions.prompt: The diagram gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, each opening and closing with a value for the lovers, + or −. A scene turns when its closing value differs from its opening value. How many of the eight scenes turn?
hints: Read each scene's opening and closing sign.
A scene that opens + and closes + does not turn.
Count the scenes whose two signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold their value.

questions.prompt: The diagram plots how high the action has climbed in each of six numbered scenes of a heist story. Which scene is the climax?
hints: Freytag's climax is the highest point of the pyramid.
Compare the heights of the scene markers.
Give the scene's number, counting from the left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

questions.prompt: In Freytag's scheme, what is the final part of a tragedy, in which the hero falls, called?
hints: The Greek word means an overturning.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The catastrophe, Freytag's 'Katastrophe'; in other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

questions.prompt: Romeo is banished at the end of 3.1, and Juliet takes the Friar's potion in Act 4. Where do these events sit on Freytag's pyramid?
hints: Do they come before or after the climax?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

flashcards.front: In 'Thou art more lovely and more temperate', what grammatical function does 'more lovely and more temperate' serve after the linking verb 'art'?
flashcards.back: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

flashcards.front: How many finite verbs are in 'When I consider how my light is spent, I fondly ask'? Count 'is spent' as one verb.
flashcards.back: Three: 'consider', 'is spent' and 'ask'.

flashcards.front: Which mark joins two independent clauses in one sentence without a conjunction and leaves their relation unstated?
flashcards.back: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

flashcards.front: What must the words before a colon form?

flashcards.front: In 'The window was broken', which participant in the action has the passive left out?

flashcards.front: In Toulmin's model, which element limits the force of a claim with words such as 'probably' or 'in most cases'?
flashcards.back: The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.

flashcards.front: Which Toulmin element states the conditions under which a claim would not hold?
flashcards.back: The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.

flashcards.front: How many years is 'four score and seven'?

flashcards.front: Which of Aristotle's three appeals works through the emotions of the audience?
flashcards.back: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

flashcards.front: 'We do not live to eat; we eat to live.' Name the figure that reverses the order of the repeated words.
flashcards.back: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

flashcards.front: What is a series of three parallel members, as in 'I came, I saw, I conquered', called?
flashcards.back: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

flashcards.front: How many syllables are in Milton's 'They also serve who only stand and waite'?
flashcards.back: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

flashcards.front: Name the metrical foot with the pattern unstressed then stressed.
flashcards.back: The iamb, as in 'com-PARE'.

flashcards.front: How many words in Keats's 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' begin with the m sound?
flashcards.back: Two: 'mists' and 'mellow'.

flashcards.front: In I. A. Richards's terms, what is the subject a metaphor describes called, as opposed to its vehicle?
flashcards.back: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

flashcards.front: In which grammatical person does a narrator write who is also a character and says 'I'?

flashcards.front: What does free indirect discourse leave out that indirect speech such as 'she thought that it was hopeless' includes?
flashcards.back: The reporting verb (the reporting clause 'she thought that').

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what is meant?
flashcards.back: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony arises when an outcome reverses the intention that produced it?
flashcards.back: Situational irony: events turn against the purpose that set them going.

A transitive verb passes its action to an object, a separate thing: rough winds shake 'the darling buds of May', and the head of that noun phrase is 'buds'. A linking verb such as 'be', 'seem' or 'become' takes a complement instead, which describes the subject itself. In 'Thou art more lovely and more temperate' the complement tells you what 'thou' is; nothing receives an action.

A clause has its own subject and finite verb. An independent clause can stand as a sentence; a dependent clause opens with a subordinator such as 'when', 'if', 'because' or 'which' and leans on another clause. In Sonnet 130, 'If snow be white' is a condition waiting for its answer. Sonnet 29 stretches the same shape across eight lines: its 'When' clause holds the speaker's misery in suspense, and the main clause, 'Haply I think on thee', arrives only at line 10.

Each finite verb anchors its own clause, so counting finite verbs is the quickest way to count clauses. 'Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds' holds three: the main clause 'Love is not love', the relative clause 'which alters', and the clause 'when it alteration finds', each with its own verb. Infinitives such as 'to serve' and participles such as 'despising' carry no tense and do not anchor a clause.

citations.claim: A comma marks a pause inside a sentence or sets off a dependent element; on its own it cannot hold two independent clauses. 'The vote was close, the motion failed' is a comma splice. Repair it with a full stop or a semicolon, or keep the comma and add a coordinating conjunction such as 'but' or 'so'. Douglass's 'You may rejoice, I must mourn' is a splice used on purpose: the abrupt join makes the two fates collide.

citations.claim: A semicolon joins independent clauses that the writer wants read as one movement of thought. It also keeps a series of clauses legible when each clause already contains a comma. Douglass states the verb once ('your celebration is a sham') and then leaves it out: 'your boasted liberty, an unholy license'. The comma marks where 'is' has been dropped, so the semicolons must do the heavier work of separating the clauses.

citations.claim: A colon follows a complete clause and promises that what comes next will explain or specify it. 'The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes' keeps that promise. A colon between a verb and its object, as in 'The reasons were: cost and delay', breaks the rule, because 'The reasons were' is incomplete. Shakespeare ends line 2 of Sonnet 18 with a colon, and the lines that follow set out why summer falls short.

In the active voice the subject performs the action: 'The committee rejected the motion.' The passive makes the receiver the subject and builds the verb from 'be' plus a past participle; the actor, if it appears at all, moves into a 'by' phrase: 'The motion was rejected by the committee.' Seven words become five when the actor returns to the front, and the sentence now opens with whoever acted.

The passive lets a writer delete the actor completely: 'Mistakes were made.' The sentence is grammatical and complete, and it assigns responsibility to nobody. That is honest when the actor is unknown or irrelevant, as in 'The temple was built in the second century'. It is evasive when the writer knows exactly who acted. Ask of every passive: who did this, and should the reader know?

A nominalisation turns an action into a noun: 'decide' becomes 'a decision', 'review' becomes 'a review of'. The noun then needs a weak verb such as 'made' or 'conduct' to carry it, and the sentence gains words while losing force. Turning the noun back into a verb restores both: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' A good test for any draft is to make the main characters subjects and their actions verbs.

Dead words carry no meaning a reader would miss. 'Personal opinion' repeats itself; 'basically' and 'final' add nothing to 'true' and 'outcome'; 'In my opinion, it is true that' only announces a claim the sentence is about to make. Cut them and sixteen words become six. Count before and after: a revision that keeps the claim and loses words is an improvement you can measure.

citations.claim: Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, from The Uses of Argument (1958), starts with the claim: the conclusion the arguer wants accepted. Grounds are the facts offered in its support, here the cracked girders. The warrant is the general rule that licenses the step from those facts to that claim: damaged girders should not carry heavy loads. Everyday arguments usually state the claim and the grounds and leave the warrant for the reader to supply.

Attacking a warrant is often stronger than attacking the grounds. Nobody disputes that the prints were on the knife; a defence lawyer asks whether prints show handling at the relevant time. When the warrant itself needs support, Toulmin calls that support backing: here, forensic research on how prints transfer and how long they last. Writing the warrant out shows you exactly what an argument assumes.

A qualifier states how strongly the claim is made: 'probably', 'in most cases', 'almost certainly'. A rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would fail: 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home'. Both make an argument harder to knock down, because they concede in advance the exceptions an opponent would raise. A claim with no qualifier is asserted as certain, and a single counterexample sinks it.

Labelling an argument means asking each statement what job it does. A particular observation is grounds. A general rule linking that observation to the conclusion is a warrant. The conclusion is the claim, and an 'unless' clause is a rebuttal. In the pricing argument the warrant is the general rule about prices, and the rebuttal allows that rising costs might justify the higher price even with fewer sales.

Lincoln builds ethos differently, with 'we': the president speaks as one of the mourners, not above them.

Lincoln's pathos is quieter: the dead gave 'the last full measure of devotion', and the living are asked to be worthy of it.

citations.claim: Logos is the argument carried by the words themselves. Lincoln's opening dates the nation to 1776 and the Declaration of Independence rather than to the Constitution of 1787, and it names the founding premise: 'all men are created equal'. The war, he reasons, tests whether a nation built on that proposition 'can long endure'. The speech argues from premise to consequence before it consoles.

Dickens keeps the frame going for ten clauses before the sentence breaks into 'we had everything before us'. Douglass uses the same device with 'your', and each repetition points back at his audience.

Antithesis places opposed ideas in parallel grammatical form, so that the parallel sharpens the opposition. Lincoln contrasts 'we' with 'they' and 'say' with 'did' inside one frame ('what ___ ___ here'), so the speech enacts its own modesty: words matter less than deeds. Dickens's 'best' and 'worst' sit in the same slot of the same clause.

A tricolon is a series of three parallel members. Lincoln's 'of the people, by the people, for the people' varies only the preposition, so each phrase adds a relation: government drawn from the people, run by them, serving them. His earlier sequence 'dedicate', 'consecrate', 'hallow' climbs from civic to sacred, a tricolon whose members grow in weight.

Scansion starts with syllables. 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' has ten, and the beats fall on the even ones: I, -pare, to, sum-, day. An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one is an iamb, and five iambs make iambic pentameter, the line of English verse drama and of the sonnet. Metrical stress need not match speech: 'to' takes a beat here only because of where it stands.

An iambic pentameter line has ten positions alternating weak and strong, so the strong positions are the even-numbered syllables. In 'Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May' the beats land on 'winds', 'shake', 'dar-', 'buds' and 'May'. Spoken English rarely gives five equal stresses. 'Rough' is heavy too, and reading it with weight against the metre is part of the line's force.

A line can carry an extra unstressed syllable after its last beat. 'That looks on tempests and is never shaken' ends 'NE-ver SHA-ken', and the final '-ken' trails off. This is a feminine ending. The line is still pentameter, because it keeps five beats; Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' has the same shape, and its unresolved last syllable suits an unresolved question.

Reverse the iamb and you have a trochee, stressed then unstressed. The witches in Macbeth chant in trochaic tetrameter, four falling feet: DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Set that beside Dickinson's iambic 'And sings the tune without the words', also eight syllables and four beats. The count is the same, but one line falls and the other rises, and Shakespeare gives his supernatural speakers a metre unlike the iambic speech of his human characters.

Alliteration repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words, usually on stressed syllables. Shakespeare's 'sessions of sweet silent thought' has three, and their hiss is the sound of quiet. Keats opens 'To Autumn' with 'mists and mellow', two m sounds that slow the line. Alliteration belongs to sound, not spelling: 'cider' and 'sorrow' alliterate, 'cider' and 'cat' do not.

Assonance repeats a vowel sound in nearby stressed syllables, whatever the consonants around it. In 'Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness' the long vowel of 'bride' returns in 'qui-', binding the urn's two names together, while 'still' and 'unravish'd' keep the short i. Shakespeare's 'new wail my dear time's waste' sounds the vowel of 'wail' again in 'waste'.

A simile compares openly, with 'like' or 'as': Burns's love is like a rose, and 'like' keeps the two apart. A metaphor identifies one thing with another: 'Juliet is the sun'. Romeo does not say she resembles the sun; he asserts it and then builds on the assertion, telling the 'fair sun' to 'kill the envious moon'. The metaphor makes a world in which its claim is true.

I. A. Richards called the subject of a metaphor its tenor and the borrowed image its vehicle. Dickinson's tenor is hope, and her vehicle is a bird she leaves unnamed at first, letting 'feathers' and 'perches' imply it until 'the little bird' of the second stanza. Wordsworth keeps his comparison explicit: 'I wandered lonely as a Cloud'. Naming tenor and vehicle lets you say exactly what a figure carries across.

Shakespeare's sonnets have fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three quatrains and a closing couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. Each quatrain brings two new rhymes, so the poem moves through seven rhyme sounds and ends on a pair. In Sonnet 18 the quatrains test the comparison with summer, and the couplet answers it: 'So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.'

citations.claim: The volta is the turn: the point where a sonnet changes direction, from problem to answer or from complaint to consolation. In the Petrarchan sonnet it usually falls where the octave gives way to the sestet. Sonnet 29 turns at that point too: eight lines of envy and self-pity, then 'Yet in these thoughts', and the speaker's state rises 'like to the lark at break of day arising'.

citations.claim: Shakespeare often delays the turn to the couplet. Sonnet 130 refuses every flattering comparison for three quatrains and turns only with 'And yet by heaven', claiming that his love is as rare as any woman 'belied with false compare'. Milton turns early, in the middle of line 8: 'But patience to prevent / That murmur, soon replies'. Where the turn falls decides how much of the poem argues and how much answers.

An omniscient narrator can generalise beyond any one mind. Pride and Prejudice opens with a 'truth universally acknowledged' and reveals in the next paragraph whose truth it is: the 'surrounding families', who regard a rich newcomer as 'the rightful property' of their daughters. The narrator borrows the neighbourhood's voice in order to expose it, and the wanting runs the other way from what the sentence claims.

By the last repetition the word has turned against Brutus, and the crowd has done the turning.
